routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is reasonable through a cumulative historical inference from Jesus' death, the reported empty tomb and appearances, witness transformations, early proclamation, and comparison with rival explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its principal historical claims are adequately supported, bodily resurrection explains their conjunction better than the live alternatives, and the evidential standard permits supernatural causation to be inferred without first assuming it.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that belief in Jesus' bodily resurrection is epistemically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish the material historical data concerning death, burial or the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and early resurrection proclamation.
Show that bodily resurrection has greater explanatory scope and power than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, error, or combinations of natural alternatives.
Show that the event's religious context and the failure of competing explanations warrant identifying the resurrection as divine action.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the historical sources through their asserted earliness, multiplicity, local detail, cultural fit, archaeology, and relevant scholarly agreement.
Defend ordinary cumulative historical reasoning against standards alleged to exclude extraordinary conclusions categorically or generate an evidential regress.

routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is unreasonable because transmitted reports, disputed historical premises, and background compatibility do not provide sufficient warrant for either the event or its supernatural cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available sources do not adequately establish the material premises, ordinary explanations or unresolved uncertainty remain live, or the evidence fails to meet the burden appropriate to an extraordinary supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the insufficiency and underdetermination of the available evidence to withholding belief in bodily resurrection as the reasonable position.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, dependent, disputed, or second- and third-hand reports cannot securely establish the proposed resurrection facts.
Show that sincerity, movement growth, accurate background details, and reported experiences remain compatible with legend, error, transmission, or unknown causes.
Require evidence not only that an unusual event occurred but also that resurrection was possible and that supernatural or divine causation produced it.
Apply an evidential burden proportionate to the extraordinariness and low background plausibility of bodily resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish reports, sincere beliefs, and incidental historical accuracy from independent support for the resurrection proposition itself.
Defend suspension of judgment without requiring a complete rival reconstruction or a claim that resurrection is impossible.

sections.title: Historical facts and source reliability
sections.rationale: The cumulative inference depends on whether death, burial, the empty tomb, appearances, conversions, and early proclamation are established by sufficiently early, independent, consistent, and reliable sources.

sections.title: Testimony, sincerity, and corroboration
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what reported experiences, costly commitment, local knowledge, archaeology, and accurate background details can establish about the central resurrection claims.

sections.title: Resurrection and rival explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether resurrection explains the proposed historical data better than legend, deception, hallucination, error, transmission, combined alternatives, or unresolved uncertainty.

sections.title: Event evidence and supernatural causation
sections.rationale: Evidence for an unusual return to life and evidence that God caused a bodily resurrection are distinct inferential questions whose connection is necessary to the motion.

sections.title: Extraordinary claims and evidential burden
sections.rationale: The appropriate relationship among prior plausibility, extraordinary claims, proportional evidence, and historical inference determines what support reasonable belief requires.

sections.title: Reasonable belief and suspension of judgment
sections.rationale: The ultimate burden requires deciding whether the cumulative case warrants belief or whether remaining evidential uncertainty makes suspension of judgment the justified motion-level conclusion.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Belief in Jesus' resurrection can be reasonable when likely historical facts are established and competing explanations of those facts are compared cumulatively.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike begins his uninterrupted opening statement at event 155 and explicitly presents this two-part case in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the two-part cumulative method and directly frames the pro motion route without answering an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the route, the historical-fact stage, and the comparative-explanation stage.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal is recoverable and expressly limited to likely facts, cumulative comparison, and reasonable belief.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims that belief can be reasonable and qualifies its method through likelihood rather than certainty.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The two stages form a coherent abductive method, though later moves must supply the historical and comparative warrants.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage clearly states the method but does not itself provide the evidence or defend the comparative criteria.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly frames the motion-level bridge from cumulative historical inference to reasonable resurrection belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: This is a methodological constructive statement and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly promises a two-part case based on likely facts of history and comparison of explanations for those facts.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by Roman crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is a securely supported historical foundation for assessing the resurrection claim.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has yielded the floor to Mike, who labels this the first fact and supports it by invoking historical sources and scholarly testimony.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies a foundational historical premise concerning Jesus' death and does not answer an earlier opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly identifies the fact, causal mechanism, Roman authority, and claimed source support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical claim is clear, although the extent and independence of the cited sources remain compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling it among the most certain historical facts slightly outruns the excerpt's authority-based presentation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-consensus considerations coherently support the crucifixion premise, with source independence left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names a scholar and eleven asserted independent sources, but does not identify or independently defend them here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Jesus' death is indispensable historical data for the central resurrection route, though it does not establish resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive passage presents affirmative historical support without engaging a developed rival interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Roman crucifixion under Pilate and invokes Ehrman's assessment plus eleven allegedly independent sources.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus was probably buried in a private tomb later found empty, supported by considerations including multiple attestation, women witnesses, Joseph of Arimathea, and archaeology.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike explicitly introduces burial and the empty tomb as his third and fourth facts, then supplies six consecutive supporting considerations and a conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops burial and empty-tomb premises through several historical considerations rather than replying to opposition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies multiple specified considerations, although their independence and cumulative weight are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition uses probabilistic language and clearly distinguishes burial, a private tomb, and its later reported emptiness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic conclusion is appropriately qualified, but some attestation and archaeology warrants remain undeveloped.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The considerations are relevant cumulatively, though the move compresses how each raises the probability of an empty tomb.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It offers named considerations and scholarship, but source independence, archaeological entailment, and rival readings remain material gaps.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Burial and an empty tomb are major historical premises central to the pro route's proposed data set.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage advances an affirmative historical case without testing a sufficiently developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span presents women witnesses, Joseph of Arimathea, multiple attestation, scholarship, and archaeology as cumulative support.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Individual and group experiences understood as appearances of the risen Jesus form historical data that ordinary hallucination does not adequately explain.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike identifies this as his fifth historical fact and develops it continuously through named accounts, scholarly consensus claims, and the hallucination inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes reported individual and group experiences and begins comparing them with hallucination as a rival.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it combines a specified historical datum with an explicit explanatory implication.

precisionFindings.rationale: It carefully frames the datum as experiences understood as appearances rather than treating the experiences alone as resurrection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical confidence in experiences is qualified, but the dismissal of ordinary hallucination lacks a full rival analysis here.

charity.alternative: The appearance reports could arise from individual visionary or hallucination experiences later generalized to groups.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must establish genuinely shared group perception rather than merely reports interpreted collectively.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between experiences and interpretation is coherent, but the group-to-nonhallucination bridge remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named scholarly agreement supports experiences, while the form and independence of group testimony remain insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Appearance experiences and their explanation directly contact the central comparative-explanation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It notes groups but does not fully address whether the source evidence independently establishes simultaneous shared perception.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites reported group perception and Lüdemann's conclusion that Peter and disciples experienced Jesus as risen.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: The disciples' transformed lives and willingness to endure persecution support the inference that they sincerely believed they had encountered the risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike continues his opening, introduces transformation as the next fact, and resumes the same argument after a brief technical interruption about his slides.

response.rationale: This constructive move supports witness sincerity through transformation and costly commitment without answering an earlier opponent.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies the limited inference to sincere belief and offers persecution as supporting evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The sincerity inference is clear, though the passage shifts between willingness to die and historically supported persecution.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Transformation supports sincerity, but willingness to die and specific martyrdom evidence are not fully separated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Costly commitment coherently supports sincerity, but sincerity does not independently validate the believed event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move invokes multiple Christian and non-Christian sources yet specifies strong support for only Peter, James, and Paul.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Sincerity materially supports the historical case but is subsidiary to whether the resurrection interpretation is true.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move argues for sincerity and does not materially characterize a developed alternative explanation of that sincerity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asserts transformed lives, willingness to suffer, multiple-source persecution, and particular support for Peter, James, and Paul.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus' religious, miraculous, and prophetic context indicates that, if he rose, the event is best understood as an act of God.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike introduces religious significance as his tenth fact and expressly draws the inference that the context identifies God as the resurrection's cause.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the proposed bridge from a resurrection event in Jesus' context to divine agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly addresses causal identification but compresses the inference from context to God.

precisionFindings.rationale: The crucial conditional qualification—if Jesus rose—is explicit and the intended causal conclusion is recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional is clear, but religious and prophetic context alone does not adequately identify divine causation.

charity.alternative: A return to life could occur for an unknown natural or nondivine reason despite a surrounding religious narrative.
charity.decisiveQualification: Context can make divine agency salient without uniquely establishing that agency as the cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Religious context is evidentially relevant, but the inference to a uniquely divine cause leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts miraculous and prophetic context without representative validation or comparison with nondivine causal alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly contacts the indispensable central bridge identifying divine causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notices the causal challenge but treats contextual fit as more discriminating than the excerpt demonstrates.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly argues that the religious context of Jesus' death and alleged rising indicates that God caused it.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Resurrection explains the cumulative historical data better than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, or combinations of those natural rival explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike explicitly shifts from listing facts to asking for their best explanation and consecutively evaluates the resurrection and several named alternatives.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly compares resurrection with conspiracy, hallucination, legend, and combined natural alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it addresses the central explanatory comparison, though the rival-by-rival warrants remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative conclusion and named rivals are clear, with the criteria for 'best' left largely implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The broad superiority claim exceeds the excerpt's abbreviated treatment of rival explanations and their combinations.

charity.alternative: Several natural processes—vision, transmission, legend, error, or combinations—could explain different parts of the proposed data.
charity.decisiveQualification: A cumulative rival need not make one mechanism explain every datum by itself.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Abductive comparison is valid in form, but explanatory criteria and the treatment of combined alternatives remain material gaps.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names and discusses rivals, yet provides limited representative support, base-rate analysis, or serious comparative testing.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central bridge requiring resurrection to outperform live rival explanations.

representationalCharity.rationale: Named rivals are considered, but the move does not fully test mixed explanations or residual uncertainty in the premises.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span shifts to best explanation and evaluates resurrection against conspiracy, hallucination, legend, and combinations.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Sincere testimony can support that an extraordinary experience was reported without sufficiently establishing that its supernatural interpretation is true.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening turn is explicitly handed to Matt immediately before the core, and the first-person family example remains within that turn.

components.text: Transformation and costly sincerity establish belief or experience, not the truth of the supernatural interpretation.
Reports that appearances occurred must be distinguished from independent evidence that resurrection caused them.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the inference from sincere reports or experiences to supernatural truth and states that reports remain claims needing further evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts and defeats the decisive testimony-to-truth inference while preserving the limited evidential value of sincerity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence of reported experience and evidence of supernatural truth is stable and explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical insufficiency claim is appropriately categorical while allowing testimony to support that experiences were reported.

charity.alternative: Sincere, multiple reports can provide some evidence for an event even if they do not entail its interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their evidential contribution still falls short of independently establishing supernatural causation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The claims-versus-support distinction is explicit, consistent, and directly blocks the stronger inference without denying all testimony.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual warrant is strong, though the excerpt does not examine the quality and independence of each report.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary bridge distinguishing claims and sincerity from support for resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the limited value of testimony and targets only the stronger supernatural inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the presented material is largely claims about resurrection and that evidence must be more than reports of experiences.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Resurrection cannot serve as the best explanation unless the possibility of supernatural interaction is supported rather than exempted from ordinary evidential standards.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Matt throughout the con opening and frames the passage in his established skeptical vocabulary of evidence, possibility, and special pleading.

components.text: Resurrection must be shown to be a viable explanatory candidate before it can win a best-explanation comparison.
Evidence must connect supernatural agency to reality rather than exempting it from ordinary standards.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges resurrection's eligibility and the causal bridge, although its demand to establish the supernatural first is itself underdefended.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive viability requirement but does not fully specify what evidence would satisfy it.

precisionFindings.rationale: 'Supernatural is real and can interact' is recoverable but leaves the relevant possibility and evidential threshold underspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some viability warrant is needed, but demanding prior proof of the supernatural risks setting the threshold too strongly.

charity.alternative: A novel cause may gain support abductively from its predicted effects without being independently established beforehand.
charity.decisiveQualification: The effects must still discriminate that cause from known and unknown alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The viability objection is relevant, but the prior-demonstration requirement risks circularly excluding abductive causal inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic standard is asserted more than defended and lacks a clear possibility or interaction test.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro bridges comparing explanations and identifying supernatural causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the legitimate discrimination problem but underplays abductive support from the event evidence itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt requires evidence that the supernatural is real and can interact with reality before treating it as an explanation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Known sources of false reports, including deception, legend, error, and exaggeration, remain better-grounded candidates than an unsupported resurrection mechanism.
moves.attributionBasis: This is still Matt's uninterrupted opening, with first-person methodological language and an explicit appeal to Hume consistent with the surrounding con argument.

components.text: Known mechanisms producing false reports remain better grounded than an unsupported resurrection mechanism.

response.rationale: The move contacts the comparative inference by contrasting known error-producing processes with an allegedly unsupported supernatural candidate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparison but does not show that any specified natural mechanism explains the complete proposed data.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is clear, although 'magic' rhetorically blurs distinct supernatural and divine-causal hypotheses.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Known false-report mechanisms deserve prior weight, but their superiority over the full case is not demonstrated here.

charity.alternative: Resurrection could provide a unified explanation with greater scope even if it has a lower prior probability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its likelihood and causal viability still require support sufficient to overcome that low prior.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prior-plausibility comparison is coherent, with a missing bridge from known mechanisms to this specific evidential conjunction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names familiar sources of false reports but supplies little case-specific evidence showing they outperform resurrection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central comparative-explanation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes comparative viability but does not fully weigh explanatory scope against prior plausibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contrasts known mechanisms and ordinary report failures with an unsupported supernatural mechanism labeled special pleading.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Noncontemporary and source-dependent accounts with unresolved inconsistencies do not securely convert the proposed minimal-facts list into established historical facts.
moves.attributionBasis: The con opening continues without interruption, and Matt explicitly names Michael, Gary Habermas, the minimal-facts approach, and his own predebate stipulations.

components.text: Late, dependent, and inconsistent accounts do not securely establish burial and empty-tomb facts.
The same source-quality problems weaken the asserted historical status of appearance reports.
The general source objection reaches the proposed fact list but gives little crucifixion-specific analysis.

response.rationale: The move attacks the source foundations of the minimal-facts-style case, but its selected excerpt provides limited item-by-item documentation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive source-sufficiency issue while only partially applying it to the particular historical claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source critique is recoverable, though it ranges broadly across the fact list without specifying which defects affect which fact.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Late dependence and inconsistency can weaken facts, but the broad conclusion needs more source-specific demonstration.

charity.alternative: Later sources may preserve early traditions and dependence does not make all their contents unreliable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Earliness and independence must be demonstrated for each material fact rather than presumed globally.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-quality inference is valid, with scope across the entire fact list left partly underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies dependence, noncontemporaneity, and inconsistency but gives limited representative source analysis in the locked span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central bridge establishing the material historical data.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly targets secure establishment, not the mere possibility that later sources preserve accurate material.

moves.evidenceBasis: The move characterizes the case as a minimal-facts variant and challenges noncontemporary, dependent, inconsistent accounts as facts.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Rejecting selected natural alternatives does not establish resurrection when information is incomplete and unknown possibilities remain, so insufficient evidence warrants uncertainty.
moves.attributionBasis: This passage forms the closing sequence of Matt's opening, ending immediately before the moderator announces the transition to dialogue and summarizes his conclusion.

components.text: Eliminating selected rivals cannot establish resurrection when the information and possibility set remain incomplete.

response.rationale: The coin-toss analogy explicitly diagnoses incomplete enumeration and states the defeating consequence: uncertainty rather than resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the core inference and identifies why elimination of listed alternatives is insufficient.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly limits its conclusion to insufficient evidence and does not claim resurrection is impossible.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force matches the underdetermination argument and explicitly preserves unknown possibilities and uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Abductive inference need not deductively eliminate every logically possible explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must nevertheless compare the strongest live alternatives and justify why residual uncertainty is acceptably small.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The incomplete-alternative-set diagnosis coherently defeats a purely eliminative inference while preserving probabilistic comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual analogy supports the inference, though its applicability depends on how comprehensively the pro case compared rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central best-explanation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets overconfident elimination while sometimes sounding broader than the proper abductive standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses incomplete coin-toss information to argue that eliminating offered options does not warrant selecting resurrection.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Detailed knowledge of Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs cumulatively corroborates the historical reliability of the Gospel reporting.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn advances the resurrection defender's case, directly addresses Matt, and is followed by Matt's explicit skeptical rebuttal.

components.text: Accurate Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs provide cumulative corroboration of Gospel historical knowledge.
Incidental accuracy can make a source more credible but does not independently prove resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply contacts general source reliability through local detail but does not answer the distinction between incidental accuracy and supernatural truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It partially answers source reliability while leaving the decisive central-claim corroboration demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Local corroboration is clear, but the passage slides from accurate detail to broad historical reliability without a scope limit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Local knowledge supports provenance or familiarity but does not strongly verify the central resurrection narrative.

charity.alternative: A source can contain accurate local detail while remaining mistaken, legendary, or dependent on its central claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: Corroboration must connect to the disputed event rather than only to background setting.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The corroboration inference has some force but overextends from incidental accuracy to broad narrative reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples of local detail are offered, yet their independence, dating, and connection to resurrection are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary source-corroboration bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply largely treats background accuracy as answering a stronger objection about central supernatural claims.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites knowledge of local details such as Zacchaeus and a sycamore tree as cumulative confirmation of reporting.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: A case combining reasonably established nonmiraculous historical facts with resurrection as their best explanation need not prove its conclusion before its supporting evidence is considered.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies his own two-part case and directly characterizes Matt's epistemic objection as circular, clearly marking Mike's turn.

components.text: The proper demand is first to assess ordinary historical facts and then compare resurrection as an explanation.
Case-specific comparison is required rather than rejecting resurrection through generalities alone.

response.rationale: The reply justifies separating premise assessment from explanatory comparison and preserves the opponent's legitimate demand for supporting evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It offers a relevant replacement demand, though it does not itself complete the evidential comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two stages and their differing evidential tasks are stated clearly and consistently.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The methodological claim that evidence must be considered before judging the conclusion is appropriately categorical.

charity.alternative: Low prior plausibility can properly affect how strongly ordinary historical facts support resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: It should affect comparative assessment without making consideration of those facts circularly unavailable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The staged distinction is coherent and avoids requiring the conclusion before considering its evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological defense is sound, though the passage does not establish that its particular facts are reasonably supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro bridge defending the evidential standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves scrutiny of both stages and fairly rejects only a standard that forecloses consideration.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly separates nonmiraculous historical facts from the later claim that resurrection best explains them.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Concluding that resurrection has not met its burden is compatible with leaving its occurrence possible and does not assume that supernatural events cannot occur.
moves.attributionBasis: The direct correction of Mike's circularity charge and the first-person statement of the skeptical conclusion identify Matt's responsive turn.

components.text: Withholding acceptance for unmet burden does not entail that resurrection is impossible or assume the conclusion.
The cumulative case may be assessed while its conclusion remains unaccepted pending sufficient support.

response.rationale: The reply defines circularity, distinguishes nonacceptance from denial, and states why the skeptical conclusion does not presuppose impossibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the circularity charge and gives the precise defeating consequence for burden assessment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among impossibility, nonoccurrence, and unmet burden is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical compatibility claim is exact and explicitly leaves the event possible.

charity.alternative: A skeptic might covertly set a standard that no historical supernatural claim could satisfy.
charity.decisiveQualification: That concern requires showing the standard is impossible, not merely noting that the present evidence fails it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply cleanly distinguishes burden failure from negation and resolves the stated circularity challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well defended, though whether the burden is actually unmet depends on the other evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge from insufficiency to reasonable nonacceptance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately limits its conclusion and directly addresses the strongest circularity interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the conclusion is unmet burden, not impossibility, nonoccurrence, or denial of supernatural events.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The reported crucifixion lacks contemporary verification, while the absence of independent reports for associated conspicuous events weakens confidence in the narrative source.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical first-person assessment follows Mike's request for agreement and invokes Matt's recurring source-verification and independent-attestation standards.

components.text: The crucifixion report lacks contemporary verification and expected independent Roman documentation.
The broader narrative's source reliability is questioned through absent independent reports of conspicuous associated events.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests verification of the crucifixion foundation, but moves from absent contemporary records to broad narrative skepticism too quickly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the historical-source demand explicitly while providing only a limited argument from expected documentation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The verification complaint is clear, but 'story book' and broad source dismissal obscure the narrower crucifixion claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Absence of contemporary accounts weakens direct verification but does not justify near-global dismissal without preservation analysis.

charity.alternative: Ancient events can be historically well supported by later sources even when contemporary records do not survive.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reliability must then depend on source proximity, independence, transmission, and external corroboration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The absence argument is relevant but relies on an underdefended expectation that the relevant records should survive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No representative survival baseline or detailed source comparison supports the broad verification conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central historical-data bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move gives insufficient weight to ordinary historical inference from later evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the narrative unverifiable, notes no contemporary biblical accounts, and expects independent Roman reporting.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Paul's language and relevant Jewish historical concepts indicate that the earliest resurrection claim concerned Jesus' bodily resurrection rather than a merely spectral experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn presents Pauline passages and a scholarly word study for the pro position before Matt objects that Mike is defending an unasserted target.

components.text: The decisive demand concerns evidential sufficiency, not whether Paul and early Jews meant bodily resurrection.
Clarifying the content of belief does not establish that the believed bodily event occurred.

response.rationale: The move supplies relevant semantic and historical material but does not contact the opponent's decisive truth-and-support distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material but remains a relevant nonanswer to the evidential-sufficiency demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim about bodily meaning is clear, though the evidence base for a uniform Jewish mentality is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: 'No way around it' overstates what the excerpt's limited word-study and cultural generalization can establish.

charity.alternative: Paul may mean bodily resurrection while his belief and reports still fail to establish that it occurred.
charity.decisiveQualification: Semantic content and historical truth are separate propositions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The semantic inference is usable, but its relevance to the live evidential objection is materially limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline language and a word study are invoked, but representative textual analysis and cultural variation are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It supports the subsidiary defense of the intended bodily claim, but not the central causal warrant.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply defends meaning against an opponent whose decisive objection concerns truth and evidential support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes a Pauline word study and Jewish concepts to insist that early believers meant bodily resurrection.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paul's third-party reports of appearances do not establish that the named witnesses personally attested as claimed or that a resurrection actually occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker resumes the answer interrupted by the Paul discussion and explicitly contrasts what Saul believed with what is true or evidentially supported.

components.text: What Paul believed resurrection meant does not establish that the bodily event actually occurred.
Paul's third-party list does not independently establish that named witnesses personally attested as reported.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies the belief-to-truth inference as invalid and states the evidential consequence for Paul's third-party reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts both the semantic argument and the underlying appearance-report support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions between Paul's belief, third-party attribution, personal attestation, and event truth are clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The nonentailment claim is appropriately categorical and does not deny that Paul's belief has historical relevance.

charity.alternative: Paul's early report may preserve testimony from people he knew and thus carry some evidential weight.
charity.decisiveQualification: That weight depends on access, accuracy, and actual witness attestation, none of which follows merely from Paul's list.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The belief-versus-truth and report-versus-attestation distinctions directly resolve the targeted inferential problem.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual warrant is strong, though the excerpt offers limited detailed analysis of Paul's access to the named witnesses.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary bridge distinguishing reports from support.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even direct confirmation that Jesus returned to life would not by itself identify either a supernatural mechanism or divine agency as the cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly identifies Matt as the respondent, and the sustained first-person answer is distinguishable from Mike's preceding hypothetical.

components.text: Confirmation that Jesus was alive again would not by itself identify how it happened or who caused it.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Bodily resurrection is an extraordinary claim whose lack of physical, contemporary, and possibility-establishing evidence leaves the available support insufficient.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly rejects Mike's characterization of his position and continues in a sustained first-person explanation of his evidential standard.

components.text: Considering ordinary historical facts does not remove the need for sufficient support for the extraordinary resurrection conclusion.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: A categorical demand for extraordinary evidence risks an evidential regress because each extraordinary item of support can itself be treated as another claim requiring further support.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike introduces the familiar extraordinary-evidence maxim, labels it circular, and develops the regress objection before yielding to Matt's response.

components.text: Treating every extraordinary item of support as a new unsupported extraordinary claim can generate an endless regress.
A burden standard should specify sufficient support without recursively excluding every possible item offered.

response.rationale: The reply contacts a categorical interpretation of extraordinary evidence, but it does not defeat the proportional-evidence interpretation actually available.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers one decisive formulation while leaving the strongest nonregressive formulation largely intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The regress conditional is clear, but 'extraordinary evidence' shifts between unusual evidence and especially strong evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Framed as a risk under a categorical demand, the regress claim is appropriately conditional.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The quantity and quality of evidence required for warranted belief should scale with a claim's extraordinariness and overcome well-supported conflicting background beliefs.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt resumes the lottery comparison, contrasts mundane and resurrection claims, and states the consequence for his broader evidential commitments.

components.text: Extraordinary evidence denotes quantity and quality scaled to the claim, not endlessly miraculous supporting claims.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Unresolved textual problems and the absence of evidence beyond resurrection reports make suspension of judgment more reasonable than accepting resurrection as an explanation.

components.text: Unresolved textual problems and evidence limited to reports leave the cumulative case insufficient for reasonable acceptance.
